newsitem.title: USA: Flotilla planned to promote Cuba work stoppage.
newsitem.headline: Flotilla planned to promote Cuba work stoppage.

text.p: Cuban exiles in boats and planes will travel to the edge of Cuban territory this weekend to promote a national work stoppage on the communist-ruled island, a prominent exile group said on Wednesday.
Democracy Movement, a Miami-based exile group, said about 35 boats and 14 planes would take part in the demonstration but none would enter Cuban territory.
The flotilla is part of a series of waterborne and airborne demonstrations planned this year in advance of Pope John Paul's scheduled visit to Cuba in 1998.

In Washington, the State Department cautioned the exiles against entering Cuban territory, territorial sea or airspace without authorisation from the Cuban government, saying they would place themselves and others "in serious danger."

Spokesman Nicholas Burns noted that Havana "proved itself willing to take actions in clear violation of international law and international aviation standards" when Cuban MiG fighter jets shot down two unarmed civil aircraft over international waters on Feb. 24, 1996.

"In the interest of avoiding unnecessary risks to all concerned, the United States government has informed the Cuban government of statements by the flotilla organisers declaring their peaceful and lawful intentions," he said in a written statement.

Burns said Washington also had made it clear it expected Havana to exercise "the utmost discretion and restraint" and not to use excessive force if any private vessels or aircraft entered Cuban waters or airspace without authorisation.

He noted that the State Department, the Federal Aviation Administration and the U.S. Coast Guard had spoken directly with the flotilla organisers and warned them of "the potentially serious consequences" of unauthorised intrusion.
Democracy Movement leader Ramon Saul Sanchez said the flotilla was designed to inform Cubans on the island of plans for a general strike, the date for which has not been decided.

Saul said exiles will not enter Cuban territory on Saturday but reserved what they called their rights as Cuban citizens to do so in the future. "They are Castro's waters and they are also our waters," he said.

The Saturday flotilla will be the latest in a series of demonstrations that have taken exiled Cubans to the 12-mile (19-km) international limit off Havana in the past three years. Cuban officials denounced the flotillas as acts of provocation.
The boats and aircraft will leave on Friday and Saturday to take up positions at three sites just outside the international limit. Prayer services will be held at the sites on Saturday afternoon.

One group of vessels will travel from Marathon Key in the Florida Keys to an area off Caibarien in central Cuba, Democracy officials said. Another will leave Key West for offshore Havana in the west of the island, and a third will leave from an undisclosed Latin American or Caribbean port for Oriente Province in the east.

Democracy Movement, which espouses nonviolent protests of communist rule in Cuba and seeks democratic reforms, planned to send exiles into Cuban territory during the pope's January visit unless Cuban President Fidel Castro publicly acknowledged their right to visit Cuba, Saul said.
"We hope to be able to exercise our right to be present in Cuba when the pope visits Cuba," he said.
